entities.summary: Wilma Pearl Mankiller was a Native American activist, social worker, community developer and the first woman elected to serve as Principal Chief of the Cherokee Nation. Born in Tahlequah, Oklahoma, she lived on her family's allotment in Adair County, Oklahoma, until the age of 11, when her family relocated to San Francisco as part of a federal government program to urbanize Indigenous Americans. After high school, she married a well-to-do Ecuadorian and raised two daughters. Inspired by the social and political movements of the 1960s, Mankiller became involved in the Occupation of Alcatraz and later participated in the land and compensation struggles with the Pit River Tribe.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: As the first woman elected to serve as Principal Chief of the Cherokee Nation, Wilma Mankiller played a crucial role in shaping tribal governance and policy. Her leadership helped to establish the Cherokee Nation as a model for Native American self-governance, with significant regional impact.
